ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Obstructed labour is the failure of a fetus to descend despite strong uterine contractions because of a mechanical block. It threatens mother and baby with necrosis, rupture, infection and death.

sections.p: When uterine activity is adequate but the fetal head does not progress through the pelvis, the labour is obstructed. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment and the partograph.
b: Adequate contractions: >200 Montevideo units or >3/10 on a visual analog scale.
No descent of presenting part for >2 h in active phase.
Caput succedaneum, edema, or molding without progress.

sections.p: The WHO partograph stages obstructed labour: latent, active, and prolonged/obstructed. Prolonged active phase (>4 h) signals severe obstruction needing urgent intervention.
b: Stage I: latent – slow progress, monitor closely.
Stage II: active – >4 h without descent = obstructed.
Stage III: complications – uterine rupture, fistula.

sections.p: Mechanical blocks are grouped by fetal, maternal‑pelvic, and iatrogenic factors. In low‑resource settings, cephalopelvic disproportion and malpresentation dominate.
b: Cephalopelvic disproportion (small pelvis, large baby).
Malpresentation: breech, transverse lie, face presentation.
Pelvic masses: fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease.
Obstetric fistula from prolonged pressure.
Iatrogenic: failed instrumental delivery, prolonged oxytocin.

sections.p: Women report strong, painful contractions but no change in fetal station. The abdomen may become tense; the presenting part may be swollen or bruised.
b: Persistent strong contractions.
No descent of presenting part on vaginal exam.
Maternal exhaustion, tachycardia.
Fetal distress: abnormal heart‑rate patterns.

sections.p: Investigations confirm adequacy of contractions, fetal well‑being and rule out other causes.

t.b: Is labour progressing as expected? A flat descent line indicates obstruction.
Is the fetus stressed? Persistent decelerations suggest compromise.
Is there a mechanical block? Failure to feel descent confirms obstruction.
What is fetal size and presentation? Large bi‑parietal diameter or malpresentation supports diagnosis.

sections.p: If untreated, obstructed labour leads to maternal and fetal catastrophe.
b: Uterine rupture – sudden abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, maternal shock.
Obstetric fistula – continuous urinary or fecal leakage after delivery.
Sepsis – fever, foul lochia, tachycardia.
Maternal hemorrhage – postpartum bleeding.

sections.p: The priority is to relieve the obstruction while protecting mother and baby. Decision‑making balances speed, resources and safety.
b: Immediate referral to a facility with surgical capacity.
If cervix fully dilated and head low: assisted vaginal delivery with forceps or vacuum (avoid if fetal head high).
If not dilated or fetal distress: emergency caesarean section.
Supportive care: IV fluids, antibiotics (broad‑spectrum covering genital flora), uterotonics after delivery, analgesia.
Treat underlying cause: e.g., manage anemia, correct electrolyte imbalance.

sections.p: After delivery, monitor for infection, bleeding and fistula formation. Long‑term prevention focuses on antenatal care and timely obstetric intervention.
b: Post‑delivery wound check, urinary testing for fistula.
Counsel on birth spacing, nutrition to improve pelvic growth.
Use partograph for all labours; refer early when progress stalls.
Educate about avoiding harmful traditional practices (e.g., female genital mutilation).

sections.p: Conditions that mimic obstructed labour but have different management.
b: Failed induction – inadequate uterotonics rather than mechanical block.
Maternal fatigue – weak contractions, not obstruction.
Fetal malposition without obstruction – may resolve with manual rotation.

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite serious obstruction.
b: Normal fetal heart‑rate baseline can hide intermittent decelerations; continuous tracing needed.
Absence of maternal fever does not exclude early sepsis; watch for tachycardia and leukocytosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Maternal tachycardia >120 bpm, severe abdominal pain, or loss of fetal station.
No progress after 2 h of strong contractions.

faq.q: Why does a strong contraction not move the baby?
faq.a: A mechanical barrier (e.g., small pelvis, breech) prevents descent despite adequate uterine force.

faq.q: Can obstructed labour be managed without surgery?
faq.a: Only if the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low enough for safe assisted vaginal delivery; otherwise surgery is required.

faq.q: What is the most common long‑term complication?
faq.a: Obstetric fistula, caused by prolonged pressure necrosis of the bladder or vagina.

exam: Describe how the partograph is used to identify obstructed labour and what action is indicated at the ‘alert’ line.
List the three most common mechanical causes of obstructed labour in low‑resource settings and explain why each leads to obstruction.
Outline the immediate management steps for a woman in active obstructed labour with fetal distress.
